claims.text: The initial near-equiatomic multi-principal-element catalyst minimizes platinum-group-metal content.
Adding approximately 0.5–1 at% Pd will create bimetallic Pd–Cu sites in the catalyst.
The Pd–Cu sites will enhance low-temperature oxidation activity.
Trace Pd doping will improve resistance to poisoning by H2O and NO.
Trace Pd doping will increase catalyst lifetime durability under transient exhaust conditions.
The proposed intervention is to integrate approximately 0.5–1 at% Pd into the alloy matrix.
The resulting Pd–Cu sites will modify the catalyst surface and microstructure.
Pd-containing active sites will facilitate adsorption and oxidation of CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures.
Pd-containing sites will mitigate strong adsorption of inhibiting H2O and NO species.
The proposed activity and poisoning-resistance effects will enhance structural stability.
Enhanced structural stability will delay performance degradation during aging.
Relative to the undoped catalyst, the Pd-doped catalyst will have a light-off temperature below 150 °C.
Relative to the undoped catalyst, the Pd-doped catalyst will provide higher CO and hydrocarbon conversion during transient operation.
Relative to the undoped catalyst, the Pd-doped catalyst will retain more activity after accelerated aging.
The unmodified multi-principal-element catalyst already has promising activity and thermal stability while using less platinum-group metal.
Prior Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu studies support enhanced low-temperature oxidation and poisoning resistance.
Benefits may not persist for exhaust compositions or operating temperatures outside the specified low-temperature transient conditions.
